vignette:
Before the summer of 2022, Rajiv had considered himself a man who could handle pressure. As a product manager for a mid-sized logistics firm in suburban New Jersey, he was known for his steady hand during quarterly launches and his ability to mediate between demanding engineers and anxious stakeholders. He and his wife, Priya, had raised two children who were now in college, and they had begun to talk about retiring early, perhaps to a quieter town. Then came the trip to visit Priya’s ailing mother in the old country—a place Rajiv had not seen in twenty years. What was supposed to be a two-week stay became a nightmare when local authorities, acting on a decades-old land dispute involving Priya’s family, detained Rajiv at a checkpoint. He was held for five days in a concrete room with no windows. The men who questioned him wore military fatigues and spoke a dialect he could barely follow. They would ask him the same questions over and over in rapid, incomprehensible chatter, and when he could not answer to their satisfaction, they would strike him, or spin him in a chair until the room tilted and he gagged. He learned to dread the sound of boots on the corridor and the siren that blared every evening from a nearby watchtower—a sound that meant the guards were changing, which often preceded another session. On the third day, they had him stand for hours until his legs gave out, and when he collapsed, one of them laughed and said something in that impenetrable tongue. Rajiv had no way of knowing what he had done wrong, and that uncertainty became a splinter lodged in his mind: There must be something about me that made this happen.

Since his release and return to the United States, Rajiv has not been able to shake the feeling that danger is still present. At home, he finds himself scanning the driveway before getting out of the car, checking that no unfamiliar vehicles are parked nearby. He has started monitoring his own body constantly—noticing when his heart beats faster, when his head feels light, when his ears ring. Any hint of dizziness sends a spike of alarm through him; he will sit down abruptly, clutch a table edge, and wait, convinced that a blackout is coming or that something worse is about to happen. Priya has learned not to touch him from behind, because he reacts with a violent flinch, sometimes knocking her hand away. He knows he is in a safe suburban house, yet he cannot relax. At night, he wakes several times—not from nightmares, but from a sense that he must check the room, listen for footsteps, confirm that the door is locked. He has come to believe that people cannot be trusted, not even the police officers he sees at the traffic light near his office. The sight of a uniform—any uniform, even a delivery driver’s—makes his throat tighten. He has changed his route to work to avoid the municipal building where officers congregate. At the grocery store, if he hears a group speaking a language he does not understand, he will abandon his cart and walk out, his pulse hammering. He tells himself it is not rational, but the feeling overrides reason.

The consequences have been concrete. Rajiv used to be the one who volunteered for high-stakes product launches; now he delegates every stressful task to junior colleagues, claiming he needs to “step back.” His manager has noticed. At a recent review, she asked if everything was all right at home, and Rajiv deflected, but he could feel the ground shifting under his career. He has stopped attending the weekly team dinners because the restaurant noise—the overlapping chatter, the clatter of dishes—feels like a room full of interrogators. Priya has begun to sleep in the guest room, not out of anger, but because his constant alertness keeps her awake. He knows she is worried, but he cannot explain to her why he is certain that nothing good can happen to him anymore.

What finally brought Rajiv to a therapist’s office was not the sleeplessness or the startle reflex, but a moment last week when he was driving home and an ambulance passed, its siren rising and falling. He pulled over, hands shaking, and sat for twenty minutes until his vision cleared. He realized then that he was losing more than sleep—he was losing the life he had built. He is afraid of what the therapy might unearth, but more afraid of the alternative: a future where every sound is a threat, and every touch is an ambush.
